posts.title: Paper first: the no-battery board that goes everywhere
posts.description: A printed board is instant, robust and easy to personalise. How to make a paper copy that matches the app and keeps communication available when technology cannot.

posts.title: Finding a voice that fits: accent, age and personality
posts.description: The voice a communication app uses is part of someone's identity. How to choose, test and personalise a voice without defaulting to the wrong one.

posts.title: Photos or symbols? Choosing what the person actually recognises
posts.description: A clear photo can work better than a neat icon, or the other way round. How to choose images by recognition rather than tidiness, and keep the board consistent.

posts.title: Signs, gestures and symbols: a total communication approach
posts.description: AAC is not one device or one method. Speech, signs, gestures, pointing and symbols can work together, and accepting every route makes communication easier.

posts.title: Modelling vs prompting: how to help without taking over
posts.description: Modelling shows someone how a board works. Prompting asks them to perform. The difference matters, and a few small habits keep help from becoming a test.

posts.title: Transitions: helping change feel manageable with AAC
posts.description: Stopping a favourite activity or moving to a new place can be the hardest part of the day. Symbols, warnings and choices can make transitions easier.

posts.title: Birthdays and celebrations: AAC in the loud, happy moments
posts.description: Parties are busy, noisy and full of relatives. A little planning helps the person using AAC join in, be understood and step out when it gets too much.

posts.title: Travel and holidays: AAC on flights, trains and unfamiliar places
posts.description: A communication system can travel, but it needs a little planning. What to pack, what to prepare and how to keep a voice available far from home.

posts.title: Reading, writing and AAC: symbols are not the enemy of literacy
posts.description: A communication board and a love of reading can grow together. Practical ways to include letters, sounds and writing without turning every moment into a lesson.

posts.title: Pain and illness: helping someone describe what hurts
posts.description: When someone cannot easily say where it hurts, behaviour is only part of the picture. How to prepare pain words, ask clearly and advocate in appointments.

posts.title: Calm-down plans: AAC for the moments after a meltdown
posts.description: When someone is overwhelmed, more words usually make things harder. How to plan a calm-down routine, keep communication available and repair afterwards.

posts.title: Friendships and playdates: AAC with children outside the family
posts.description: Friends usually adapt quickly when they know what to do. Simple preparations help a child with AAC join in, be understood and stay in charge of their own voice.

posts.title: Teasing, bullying and self-advocacy: words that help at school
posts.description: A communication device can attract unwanted attention. How to prepare clear words, involve the school and support a child or teenager to speak up for themselves.

posts.title: Teenagers and AAC: privacy, independence and a voice of their own
posts.description: Adolescence changes everything, including communication. How to involve a teenager in choosing their vocabulary, voice and boundaries without hovering.

posts.title: Dating and relationships with AAC: love, consent and boundaries
posts.description: Adults and teenagers who use AAC have the same right to relationships as anyone else. How to make room for dating, privacy and clear consent.

posts.title: AAC at work: meetings, interviews and everyday colleagues
posts.description: A communication system belongs in the workplace too. Practical ways to prepare for meetings, ask for adjustments and keep a professional voice.

posts.title: Build it together: co-designing the board with the person who uses it
posts.description: A board works better when the person has a say in it. Practical ways to involve children, teenagers and adults in choosing words, images and layout.

posts.title: When the device isn't being used: a troubleshooting checklist
posts.description: A communication app that sits unused is not a failed experiment. Work through access, motivation, vocabulary and partner habits before changing the whole system.

posts.title: Charging, cleaning and backups: looking after a communication device
posts.description: A few simple habits keep a device working, protect custom words and photos, and avoid the panic of a flat battery at the wrong moment.

posts.title: Waiting for an assessment or funding: what you can do meanwhile
posts.description: Waiting lists can be long, and starting AAC should not depend on a perfect plan. Practical steps to take while you wait for professional or financial support.

posts.title: The ten-second pause: the communication skill most of us skip
posts.description: Waiting feels awkward, but a quiet pause often does more for communication than another question. What to try, and how it fits with modelling.

posts.title: Starting school with AAC: a handover that actually helps
posts.description: A one-page profile, a short demonstration and a few agreed words can make the difference between a device that is used at school and one that stays in the bag.

posts.title: No, stop, help: teaching control and consent with AAC
posts.description: A communication system is not only for asking. The words that let someone refuse, change their mind and ask for help matter just as much.

posts.title: More than “more”: comments, feelings and jokes with AAC
posts.description: Requesting is only one reason to communicate. Comments, feelings, protests and silly moments are what make a voice feel like a person.

posts.title: Small words, big difference: why core words matter
posts.description: Words like I, want, stop, go and help do more work than a hundred nouns. How to choose and model core vocabulary without turning it into a lesson.

posts.title: Keep it within reach: access is part of communication
posts.description: A communication device only works when it is there. Practical ways to keep it charged, close and available without turning it into a reward.

posts.title: When every tap seems random: respond first, correct later
posts.description: Exploring a symbol board can look like chaos. What the tapping might mean, and how to respond without turning communication into a test.

posts.title: Siblings and AAC: making room for everyone's voice
posts.description: Brothers and sisters are often the best communication partners, and sometimes the most overlooked. How to include them without making them carers.

posts.title: Explaining AAC to grandparents and relatives without a lecture
posts.description: A one-sentence explanation, three words to model and permission to get it wrong can turn a well-meaning relative into a confident communication partner.

posts.title: Play, pause and sabotage: low-pressure ways to model
posts.description: Games create reasons to communicate without a worksheet. How to use people games, waiting and gentle sabotage to make symbols feel useful.

posts.title: Mealtimes: the easiest place to start with AAC
posts.description: Food brings choices, repetition and a natural reason to communicate. How to use breakfast, snacks and dinner without turning the table into a lesson.

posts.title: Books, songs and repetition: building words through favourites
posts.description: A familiar story or song gives the same words again and again. Simple ways to model symbols during reading and music without turning either into a test.

posts.title: Out and about: parks, shops and appointments with AAC
posts.description: A little planning makes communication easier away from home, from the playground to the GP surgery. What to pack, what to model and what to prepare.

posts.title: Choosing words that sound like the person
posts.description: A board should fit a real life, not a generic list. How to choose vocabulary around interests, age, culture and the words a person actually needs.

posts.title: When progress feels slow: what to notice besides words
posts.description: AAC progress is often quiet. Signs to look for, how to keep simple notes, and when to ask for a review instead of blaming yourself.

posts.title: Working with a speech and language therapist on AAC
posts.description: What to bring, what to ask and how to make appointments useful when you are introducing a communication system at home.

posts.title: AAC in multilingual families: keep the home language close
posts.description: A communication board should not flatten a family into one language. How to make room for home language, names, food and the words that feel like home.

posts.title: AAC is not only for children: adults after stroke and with changing needs
posts.description: Adults use AAC too, sometimes after a stroke, an injury or a progressive condition. Respect, fatigue and a voice that fits an adult life matter.

posts.title: Privacy and dignity: AAC in personal care and public places
posts.description: A communication device holds private words, photos and messages. How to protect dignity, ask before sharing and keep the person in control.

posts.title: Emergency communication: plan beyond the app
posts.description: A communication app can fail, run out of battery or be out of reach. A simple backup plan helps someone ask for help when it matters most.

posts.title: Everyday routines: small moments to communicate
posts.description: Mealtimes, getting dressed, play and bedtime bring up the same words again and again. Ideas for using those moments with a symbol board.

posts.title: Modelling: showing, not testing
posts.description: How families use their child's symbol board themselves while they talk, and simple ways to fit it into an ordinary day.

posts.title: What is augmentative and alternative communication (AAC)? A plain-language introduction for parents
posts.description: What augmentative and alternative communication means, the forms it takes, and the worries parents raise most often.

posts.title: Sono, honestly: where the project stands
posts.description: What Sono is, what works today, what doesn't work yet, and how you can help as a volunteer.
